claims.text: Engineered interfaces between alternating HEA layers act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Engineered interfaces particularly impede dislocation climb.
Intrinsic lattice distortions are characteristic of HEAs.
Intrinsic lattice distortions in HEAs reduce dislocation mobility.
The combined effects of interfaces and intrinsic lattice distortion reduce creep deformation.
Decreasing the multilayer modulation period increases interface density.
Increasing interface density creates a greater cumulative barrier to dislocation motion.
HEA multilayers with greater interface density will have lower creep rates than monolithic HEA coatings of the same overall composition.
HEA multilayers with greater interface density will enter tertiary creep later than monolithic HEA coatings.
HEA multilayers with greater interface density will have longer creep lifetimes than monolithic HEA coatings.
Creep is a relevant deformation mode for HEAs at elevated temperatures in the proposed 500–1000 °C range.
The interface-density effect on creep may depend on interface bonding quality.
The interface-density effect on creep may depend on interfacial chemistry.
Residual-stress distributions may influence the creep response attributed to interface density.
If interfaces impede dislocations, deformation should produce a detectable difference in dislocation accumulation at or near interfaces.
The proposed interfacial barrier mechanism is supported by analogous findings in conventional metallic multilayers and monolithic HEAs.
